summary:
The Further Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024 (Public Law 118-47, enacted March 23, 2024) provides funding for the federal government for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2024. It is organized into seven divisions (A–G) covering the Department of Defense; Financial Services and General Government; Homeland Security; Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education; the Legislative Branch; State and Foreign Operations; and Other Matters. Under Section 3, references to "this Act" within a division apply only to that division unless stated otherwise, and Section 4 gives an accompanying explanatory statement in the Congressional Record the effect of a joint conference report. Emergency-designated funds become available only if the President subsequently designates them (Section 6), and Members of Congress receive no cost-of-living adjustment for FY2024 (Section 7).

Division A funds the Department of Defense. Military personnel appropriations include $50,041,206,000 for the Army, $36,707,388,000 for the Navy, $15,268,629,000 for the Marine Corps, $36,204,130,000 for the Air Force, and $1,256,973,000 for the Space Force, with additional amounts for Reserve and National Guard components. Operation and maintenance receives large sums including $71,972,007,000 for the Navy, $61,471,101,000 for the Air Force, and $52,599,068,000 for Defense-Wide activities. Numerous general provisions restrict or condition spending—for example, limits on transferring armor-piercing ammunition, reporting requirements for new defense innovation projects exceeding $5 million, and $100,000,000 for AFRICOM/SOUTHCOM cooperation subject to advance notification. Funds are provided for Fisher Houses and related purposes.

Division B (Financial Services and General Government) funds the Treasury and the Executive Office of the President, including $78,904,000 for the White House, $129,000,000 for the Office of Management and Budget, and $298,579,000 for the High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas program (available through September 30, 2025). Government-wide provisions bar funds for pornography-accessible networks, restrict conference spending over $500,000, prohibit certain SEC political-contribution disclosure rules, and require transparency statements on federally funded communications and grants. Rescissions include $387,500,000 from the Treasury Forfeiture Fund and multiple American Rescue Plan Act amounts ($10 million, $100 million, and $283 million).

Division C funds the Department of Homeland Security, including Secret Service, CISA, and FEMA. FEMA Federal Assistance totals $3,497,019,369, allocated among grant programs such as $553,500,000 for the Urban Area Security Initiative, $468,000,000 for State Homeland Security Grants, and $648,000,000 for firefighter and SAFER grants.

Division D funds Labor, HHS, and Education. Labor provisions amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to exempt certain disaster-claims adjusters from overtime for two years after a major disaster (effective on enactment) and modify H-2B visa rules for seafood and wage determinations. HHS provisions allow Indian tribes and migrant/seasonal agencies to set Head Start enrollment priorities, and rescind $1,250,000,000 from the Nonrecurring Expenses Fund by September 30, 2024. Education receives $19,107,790,000 for Education for the Disadvantaged, $1,625,151,000 for Impact Aid, and $5,776,178,000 for School Improvement Programs.

Division E funds the Legislative Branch, including $588,627,000 for Capitol Police salaries (overtime capped at $74,976,000), $70,000,000 for the Congressional Budget Office, and Architect of the Capitol accounts. It prohibits purchasing PRC-affiliated drones except for national security.

Division F funds State and Foreign Operations, including $983,250,000 for the Development Finance Corporation (with a $12,000,000,000 loan ceiling) and $87,000,000 for the Trade and Development Agency. Provisions bar moving the Israel embassy from Jerusalem, extend the Afghan Allies Protection Act (increasing visas to 50,500 through December 31, 2025), require Ukraine oversight with 50% cost-matching and periodic reporting, prohibit funds to the central Government of Russia, and provide at least $300,000,000 for the Countering Russian Influence Fund.

Division G addresses other matters, including reauthorization of the Udall Foundation, a limitation on UNRWA funding, and budgetary effects.
